title: GRE tunnel health checks and failover

prose.text: A GRE tunnel that is up on the router can still be useless, so health has two layers. {{keepalive-limit}} {{monitoring-required}} {{health-checks}} {{no-popular-site-checks}}
The tunnel design itself (primary and secondary in different data centers) is in [[zia.traffic-forwarding.gre]].

checks.do: Which failover profile the router runs, Fast or Conservative.
Whether the health check targets the Zscaler VPN test URL rather than a public site.
Whether the track is wired to the route, since failover happens only when monitoring drives it.

monitoring-required.statement: Zscaler requires monitoring of GRE tunnels, with monitoring tied to failover: when service monitoring is down the primary tunnel fails over to the backup, and it switches back when monitoring recovers.

quotes: Zscaler requires you to monitor your GRE tunnels so that failover between the primary and the backup tunnels is triggered if a tunnel goes down.
Zscaler requires you to connect tunnel monitoring to tunnel failover.
When service monitoring is down, the primary tunnel should fail over to the backup tunnel, and when monitoring is available, switch back to the primary tunnel.

keepalive-limit.statement: GRE interfaces have no built-in way to detect a tunnel failure, so GRE keepalives are configured on the physical or logical interface; they monitor the interface, not the service beyond it.

quotes: GRE tunneling interfaces do not have a built-in mechanism for detecting when a tunnel fails.
However, the GRE keepalives monitor the interface, not the service beyond the interface.
Therefore, configure GRE keepalives on the physical or on the logical interface to detect tunnel failures.

health-checks.statement: Service monitoring uses Layer 7 health checks where the vendor supports them (Cisco IP SLA, some Juniper devices through RPM), otherwise Layer 4 checks such as ICMP and PAC-based failover. The check is an HTTP raw request to http://gateway.<Zscaler cloud>.net/vpntest.

quotes: deploy Layer 7 health checks if your vendor supports it. If your vendor does not support Layer 7 health checks, deploy Layer 4 health checks, such as ICMP and PAC-based failover.
The majority of Cisco devices support Layer 7 health checks using IPSLA and some Juniper devices support health checks using RPM
send an HTTP raw request to the following URL: http://gateway.<Zscaler cloud>.net/vpntest.

no-popular-site-checks.statement: Do not run Layer 7 health checks against commonly visited sites such as www.google.com: Google may denylist the service's IP addresses and enforce CAPTCHA on every user behind them.

quotes: Do not perform Layer 7 health checks on commonly visited websites like www.google.com. This may cause Google to place Zscaler's IP addresses on their denylist and enforce the Google CAPTCHA on all users coming from those IP addresses.

failover-profiles.statement: Zscaler publishes two failover profiles. Fast: keepalive 10 3 (30 seconds), ICMP echo every 10 seconds, track delay down 30 and up 45 seconds, best case 30-32 seconds and worst case 40-42 seconds, higher false-positive risk and CPU use, Layer 3 only. Conservative: keepalive 30 4 (120 seconds), HTTP raw every 60 seconds, delay down 120 and up 180 seconds, best case 120-125 and worst case 180-185 seconds, lower false-positive risk, tests the HTTP service.

quotes: | GRE Keepalive | Keepalive 10 3 (30 seconds failure) | Keepalive 30 4 (120 seconds failure) |
| Best-Case Failover | 30–32 seconds | 120–125 seconds |
| Worst-Case Failover | 40–42 seconds | 180–185 seconds |
| False Positive Risk | Higher | Lower |
| Application Layer Test | No (Layer 3 only) | Yes (HTTP service) |
| IP SLA Type | ICMP Echo | HTTP Raw |
| IP SLA Frequency | 10 seconds | 60 seconds |
| Track Delay Down | 30 seconds | 120 seconds |
| Track Delay Up | 45 seconds | 180 seconds |
| CPU/Resource Usage | Higher | Lower |

delay-down-up.statement: In the conservative example the router probes once every 60 seconds, marks the test down after 120 seconds (two consecutive failures) and up after 180 seconds (three consecutive successes), so short flaps do not trigger failover.

quotes: This means that the router waits for two consecutive failures before marking the connection as down, and it waits for three consecutive successes before marking the connection as up.
The delay down command prevents frequent failovers due to short-lived flaps in the connection.
This command ensures that the failover happens only when multiple connection drops are observed consecutively.

In the following example, the delay time to mark an IP SLA test as down is configured as 120 seconds. The delay time to mark an object as up is configured as 180 seconds. The router generates an HTTP SLA probe once every 60 seconds.
